claims.text: A native iron oxide passive film governs the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
At room temperature, the passive film forms slowly.
At room temperature, the passive film remains stable and suppresses further corrosion.
At elevated temperature, the passive film forms rapidly.
Elevated temperature thermally destabilizes the passive film, leading to localized pitting and accelerated corrosion.
The pre-exposed Q235 steel has an initially formed native oxide layer.
Passive-film integrity and compositional stability mediate the effect of exposure temperature on corrosion behavior.
Slower oxide-formation kinetics at room temperature permit development of a compact, defect-minimized passive layer.
The compact, defect-minimized passive layer protects Q235 steel against further corrosion.
Faster oxide growth at elevated temperature initially produces a thicker film.
Thermal stresses at elevated temperature create microstructural defects and destabilize the passive layer.
Defects and destabilization of the passive layer trigger localized pitting and accelerated corrosion degradation.
Q235 specimens exposed at 60°C will show more degraded passive-film structure than the reference.
Q235 specimens exposed at 60°C will show higher pitting density than the reference.
Q235 specimens exposed at 60°C will show increased corrosion rates relative to the reference.
The proposed mechanism applies under static, non-mechanically stressed conditions to Q235 steel bearing native oxide films.
Variations in alloy composition or additional stress factors may alter passive-film behavior and the resulting corrosion outcomes.
A controlled comparison of identical specimens at approximately 25°C and 60°C, with humidity, atmosphere, and duration held constant, is proposed to isolate the effect of temperature.

Failure to observe statistically significant film degradation, increased pitting, and increased corrosion at 60°C relative to the room-temperature exposed specimens would falsify the proposed elevated-temperature mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome names an untreated room-temperature specimen kept in standard laboratory atmosphere as the reference, whereas the experimental design and falsification rule compare the 60°C specimen with a room-temperature specimen exposed to the same harsh environment. These are different controls and can yield different causal comparisons.
